00 Platform primer

Back to contents

This page gives the background every feature file assumes: what the services are, how a request reaches them, how errors look, and the microservice ideas the code relies on. The ideas are explained in explainer boxes (📦) below; feature files link here instead of repeating them.

1. The platform in one paragraph

GoBCB sells and checks tickets for Bangladesh Cricket Board events. Staff set up programs (a series or a tournament), the venues (stadium → gallery → block → level), the events (matches) with prices and capacity, promotions and ticket layouts in the admin portal. Customers browse and buy on the user web portal or the user app, pay through DgePay, and receive digitally signed PDF tickets with a QR code. Gate staff scan the QR codes offline with the checker app. The backend is a set of ASP.NET Core 8 web APIs ("services") in one repository, running on Amazon EKS behind API Gateway (see gobcb-aws-architecture.md §0–§4).

2. Backend services

All services live in rvl-gobcb-backend/Services/<Name>/, each split into ETP.<Name>.Service (controllers, Program.cs, workers), .Domain (managers = business logic), .Storage (EF Core DbContext, repositories) and, for some, .Client (typed HTTP client other services use) and .Integration. Shared code is in rvl-gobcb-backend/Core/ (ETP.Core, ETP.Core.Web, …).

The hosting part of this picture (API Gateway, NLB, ingress) comes from the architecture document §1 and §4.1. Whether API Gateway also validates tokens is reported but unverified there (architecture Q1/Q1b). The services always validate the token themselves.

📦 Explainer: path-prefix routing

In a monolith every controller lives under one host. Here each service is a separate process, but clients still use one API host. The first path segment decides which service gets the request: /booking/api/v1/user-booking-order goes to Booking, /event/api/v1/events/list to Event.

Two pieces make this work: 1. In the code, Core/ETP.Core/Conventions/GlobalRoutePrefixConvention.cs prepends Application:ServiceName to every controller route (registered in each Program.cs, for example Services/Booking/ETP.Booking.Service/Program.cs:51). So the Booking controller's [Route("api/v1/user-booking-order")] is really served at /booking/api/v1/user-booking-order, even when you call the service directly on its own port. 2. In the cluster, an nginx ingress per service forwards /<prefix>/... to that service unchanged (architecture §4.1).

Consequence for you: when you call a service locally (http://localhost:5102), you must still include the prefix: http://localhost:5102/booking/api/v1/.... Swagger is at /<prefix>/swagger.

5. Request and response conventions

Topic What the code does Source
JSON property names camelCase in every service. Booking, Event, Ticketing, TicketChecker, Scheduler, Utility, PushNotification, Platform and UserAuth set PropertyNamingPolicy = CamelCase explicitly; Admin and UserIssue use the ASP.NET Core default, which is also camelCase Services/*/ETP.*.Service/Program.cs (AddJsonOptions)
Enums Strings (JsonStringEnumConverter) in the services that call AddJsonOptions; numbers in Admin and UserIssue, which do not register the converter same
Nulls Omitted from responses (WhenWritingNull) in the services that call AddJsonOptions; Admin and UserIssue include them same
Errors ErrorResponseExceptionFilter turns exceptions into ProblemDetails (see below) Core/ETP.Core.Web/Filters/ErrorResponseExceptionFilter.cs
Ids Most tables use a long Id. Many also carry a public string/Guid id (for example Event.EventId, order PublicId), and endpoints accept one or the other, which is why pairs such as events/{eventId} and events/EventLongId/{id} exist Services/Admin/ETP.Admin.Storage/Models/Event.cs
Time Server-side comparisons use DateTime.UtcNow e.g. UserBookingOrderManager.cs:1135-1193

Error responses. Controllers throw; the filter maps the exception type to a status code and a ProblemDetails body:

Exception Status Body
ArgumentException (and subclasses) 400 { "status": 400, "title": "<exception message>" }
ApiException 400 the exception's own Details (ProblemDetails)
UnauthorizedAccessException 403 { "status": 403, "title": "Unauthorized access", "detail": "<message>" }
anything else 500 { "status": 500, "title": "An unexpected error occurred." } (the real message in Development)

In the Development environment a stackTrace field is added. Authentication failures (no or invalid token) never reach the filter: the JWT handler answers 401 with an empty body; a valid token from the wrong pool or without the role answers 403.

{
  "status": 400,
  "title": "Invalid promo code. Please enter a valid code."
}

6. Explainer boxes

📦 Explainer: token forwarding (how one service calls another for a user)

When a customer's request reaches Booking and Booking needs data from Event, Booking calls Event over HTTP. In this code base that call carries the customer's own Cognito access token, not a service identity.

  • Each service registers typed HttpClients (for example services.AddHttpClient<IEventClient, EventClient> in Services/Admin/ETP.Admin.Service/Configurations/DependencyConfig.cs:123) with a base URL from Services:<Name>.
  • The client pipeline includes DelegatedBearerAuthenticationHandler (Core/ETP.Core.Web/Security/DelegatedBearerAuthenticationHandler.cs). It reads the access token that the JWT handler stored as a claim on the current user (OnTokenValidated in Core/ETP.Core/Configuration/DefaultAuthenticationConfig.cs) and copies it to Authorization: Bearer on the outgoing request.
  • The downstream service validates that token again with its own policy. If Booking calls an Admin endpoint that requires the Admin pool while the caller is a customer, the downstream call fails with 401/403.
  • Retries: most clients retry 3 times with exponential backoff (Polly).
  • No user, no token. A background worker has no HTTP request, so the handler finds no token and sends none. That is why the endpoints workers call have no [Authorize] (see X-18).

Hop tags: [HTTP + user token] and [HTTP, no token]. Full details: X-19.

📦 Explainer: queue-driven processing (SQS)

Some work is too slow or too important to do inside the user's request: signing a ticket with the TSP, merging hundreds of PDFs, recording VAT with NBR, sending push messages, recalculating capacity. The request publishes a message to an Amazon SQS queue and returns; a worker in some service reads the queue later and does the work.

  • Publishing: Core/ETP.Core/Queue/Services/SqsPublisher.cs resolves the queue URL from its name (configured as AWS:Queue:<Key>), serializes the message as JSON and sends it. If the queue name ends in fifo, it also sets MessageGroupId and MessageDeduplicationId from the message.
  • Consuming: a BackgroundService loops, calls ReceiveMessageAsync, processes, and deletes the message only on success. A failed message becomes visible again and is retried.
  • Messages hold business ids only. There is no user token in a message and no sender check: anyone with IAM permission to send to the queue can enqueue work (architecture §2.3 C).
  • Queue keys used: OrderSuccess, EventCapacity, VatChallanProcessing (Booking), TicketSigning (Ticketing), TicketProcessing (Utility), FirebaseNotification (Scheduler).
  • MassTransit is registered in some services but no consumer or publisher uses it (see Appendix A).

Hop tag: [SQS: Key]. Feature files in 50-system-initiated describe each consumer.

📦 Explainer: background workers (timers inside services)

Besides answering HTTP requests, several services run hosted services (BackgroundService) on a timer, registered with services.AddHostedService<...>(). The pattern is the same everywhere (Services/Admin/ETP.Admin.Service/Workers/BackgroundServices/CheckedTicketService.cs):

  1. wait about a minute after start-up;
  2. loop forever: try to take a Redis lock, and if it is taken, create a DI scope and run a TaskManager (Workers/TaskManagers/*) that holds the real logic;
  3. sleep for a hard-coded interval (30 seconds to 1 day), longer after an error.

The intervals are constants in the code, not configuration. Every replica (pod) of a service runs the same workers, which is why the lock matters (next box). Hop tag: [Worker: interval, lock].

📦 Explainer: distributed locks (RedLock)

In production each service can run as several pods. Without coordination, every pod's worker would process the same orders at the same time. The code uses RedLock (RedLockNet) on Redis: before a job runs, the worker asks for a named lock (for example checked_ticket, expiry 20 minutes). Only the pod that gets it does the work; the others skip the cycle and log Could NOT acquire lock ... Skipping this cycle (a normal message, also seen locally).

The same mechanism protects business operations that must not overlap, for example one booking at a time per customer (user_booking:{userId} in UserBookingOrderManager.cs:68) and capacity changes per level.

Set-up: Core/ETP.Core/Configuration/DistributedLockConfig.cs (keys DistributedLock:Redis:*). Lock names and expiries are listed in X-25.

📦 Explainer: one database, shared tables and read models

A textbook microservice owns a private database. This code base does not work that way:

  • Every DbContext uses the same schema etp (DefaultSchema = "etp" in each *DbContext.cs), and each service has its own connection-string key (ConnectionStrings:Admin, :Booking, …). Ticketing uses ConnectionStrings:Booking. Locally all keys point at one database, etp_local (scripts/user-secrets.example.json).
  • A table is owned by the service whose migrations create it. Other services map the same table again in their own DbContext with ExcludeFromMigrations, and read it (sometimes write it) directly. Example: Booking maps PromoCodes, Discounts, EventVenueDetails, Events from Admin as excluded tables (Services/Booking/ETP.Booking.Storage/DbContexts/BookingDbContext.cs:86-140).
  • The Event service owns almost nothing: it is a public, read-only view over Admin's and Booking's tables (Services/Event/ETP.Event.Storage/DbContexts/EventDbContext.cs).

What this means for you: a column change in Admin can break Booking, Ticketing or Event at run time even though they compile separately. Search all *DbContext.cs files for a table name before you change it. The brief we received says "one schema per service"; the code says one schema for all. The production layout is open: [UNCONFIRMED: Q-02].

Hop tag: [Shared table].

📦 Explainer: Redis as the live seat counter

Seat availability changes every second during a sale, so Booking keeps live counters in Redis (key families such as level_live, level_locked, event_live, level_live_seats; constants in Core/ETP.Core/Constant/AppConstant.cs:64-104) and treats the database as the slower, durable copy. Orders lock capacity in Redis first; queue workers (S-01, S-02) and timers (S-03) bring the database and Redis back in line. The gate-scan counters of the checker app work the same way (C-05, S-14).

Consequence: if Redis is flushed during a sale, live numbers are rebuilt from the database by the next worker cycle; locally scripts/Seed-EtpData.ps1 clears the cache for this reason. Details: X-25.
